Review:
The problem is well posed at the descriptive level and poorly posed at its headline level. The calibration and threshold tables can support a credible two-rotor bias/gain decomposition: 67 calibration rows across three nominal springs give tight linear fits and negligible loading–unloading gaps, so the “geometry, not spring nonlinearity” constraint is defensible. The 40 threshold rows are adequate to estimate, for pair_A, how window centre and half-width vary with ℓ (four values, two rotors, both neighbour states, both directions). The claimed pattern — width roughly preserved across neighbour states, centre shift growing with ℓ, much larger bias in the crossed pair_B — is a measured relation, not yet a mechanism, and the problem mostly labels it as such.

The central difficulty is the four-rotor test. Sixteen events are two repetitions of eight states, hence eight transitions, and every transition changes one rotor. That is enough to describe a cycle but not to “reproduce” it with a pairwise hysteron model: network_C connectivity, stop angles, attachment coordinates and reversal values are absent, and the state_event rows have no direction column. Without knowing whether each event occurred on increasing or decreasing drive, even the up/down threshold assignment in C is underdetermined; the instruction not to infer reversals from extrema removes the remaining shortcut. So a forward simulation of the C cycle would rest on assumptions that the data cannot check. The problem’s own “unknowns to preserve” section implicitly concedes this, but the stated goal still promises a reproduction test. That mismatch is the main feasibility risk.

Two further weaknesses reduce leverage. First, P1 cannot be tested on the supplied data: pair_B has ℓ fixed at 4.7 cm, so “sweeping ℓ in a crossed device” is a new experiment, not an analysis of these rows. Second, P4 is close to tautological: two identical cycles under one drive protocol show repeatability, not attractor stability under amplitude perturbation. The tie pairs at 5.8/5.8 and −5.1/−5.1 also make the nominal order 1,3,4,1,2,4,3,2 partly conventional; the within-tie order is not identified.

Rating: 3.

Feedback:
Reframe the deliverable as (i) a two-rotor decomposition using pair_A, with pair_B as an out-of-sample structural check rather than an ℓ sweep; (ii) an explicit identifiability statement for C — enumerate graph/reversal/direction assignments consistent with the eight transitions, and report the equivalence class rather than a unique graph; (iii) a discrimination analysis naming the minimal measurement that shrinks that class. That is feasible with the present rows. The forward “reproduce the four-rotor cycle” claim should be demoted to a conditional prediction contingent on acquiring reversal positions, direction labels, and single-rotor thresholds in C.

Fix the bookkeeping before modelling. Publish the sign convention that maps “up/down” to drive direction and state change; the rotor 2 pair_B case (down at γ=+2.1 with other=−1; both thresholds positive at ℓ=4.731) is not necessarily anomalous but will be misread unless the offset-torque convention is explicit. Treat the two tie events as order-ambiguous and analyse both admissible orders; do not present 1,3,4,1,2,4,3,2 as uniquely measured. Count free parameters against constraints: eight transitions, each at best an inequality on one rotor threshold, cannot identify six pair couplings plus attachment geometry, so state that null result plainly.

For P2, the ℓ² claim rests on four ℓ values, only three nonzero, in one device. Fit centre shift versus ℓ with an explicit offset and report a slope interval, not a point exponent; test the ℓ² form against a linear alternative. For P1 and P3, label them as proposed measurements whose apparatus feasibility is unknown, not as tests available here. Keep the measured relations (width invariance across neighbour state, centre shift growth, large crossed-pair bias) separate from the proposed lever-arm mechanism; the mechanism is plausible but currently unfitted. With these changes the problem becomes a bounded, honestly negative-capable identifiability study, which is genuinely feasible; without them it invites overstatement from sparse, direction-poor events.
